observed_mechanics: 0x00b3d850/0x00b3d86e PUSH/POP ESI is the only frame work; the function has no locals and cannot spill, so every intermediate value must live in EAX, EAX again, or memory.

0x00b3d853 ADD dword ptr [ESI],0x4 is a read-modify-write of the cursor field itself, not of a register copy. Advancing through the memory location is what lets the loop run without any register-held induction variable.

0x00b3d856/0x00b3d858/0x00b3d85b reload the cursor into EAX and compare it against the end pointer at +0x04. The comparison is JZ, so the loop stops on an exact pointer equality with the end pointer, not on a count or an ordering.

The advance precedes the end test, so the slot the handle started on is never examined: the first element considered is always the one after the incoming cursor. This is the loop's most important invariant and it is a property of the instruction order, not of any test.
0x00b3d85d MOV EAX,dword ptr [EAX] dereferences the cursor to obtain the element, and 0x00b3d85f pushes it as the single stack argument to the port.

0x00b3d860 LEA ECX,[ESI+0x8] loads the owner slot into ECX, but the port's live disassembly (23 instructions) never reads ECX - it reads its argument from [ESP+0x4] at 0x00c02600. The owner load is therefore dead with respect to this call, and is recorded as observed rather than interpreted.

0x00b3d868 TEST AL,AL with 0x00b3d86a JZ back to 0x00b3d853 fixes the polarity: a ZERO result from the port means keep advancing, a NON-ZERO result means stop. Two independent callers confirm this reading, because they call the port themselves and branch on a non-zero result to keep the current element.
0x00b3d86c MOV EAX,ESI is reached from the exhaustion branch and by falling out of the loop, so both paths return the receiver and the port's answer never leaves the function.
The port 0x00c02600 is 23 instructions ending in RET 0x4, so it pops the one word this function pushes and the loop's stack depth is constant across iterations.

There is no guard for an incoming handle whose cursor already equals its end. The loop will step past the end pointer and keep dereferencing, because the end test is equality rather than ordering. Both inspected callers set up the handle so that the cursor starts strictly before the end, so the original relies on its callers.
0x00b3d850 appears nowhere in .rdata or .data as a dword (scan total=0), so it is a non-virtual free-standing helper with no vtable presence.

sibling_analysis.question: what is this function part of?
sibling_analysis.answer: It is a compiler-emitted iteration helper for a three-word cursor handle, called from 18 sites. The 0x00B3D330-0x00B3D620 run immediately below it is a block of Simulator service getters (cSimulatorSystem::Get through cCommManager::Get, 19 named entries in the SDK symbol table), and 0x00b3d850 sits 0x230 bytes past Simulator_GetModelWorld, the last of them. It is therefore NOT a service accessor and NOT part of that accessor family.
sibling_analysis.inlined_duplicates: 0x00b41a40 and 0x00d66600 both contain hand-inlined fragments of exactly this advance-and-test loop, the latter at 0x00d666d3-0x00d666fc with the same TEST AL,AL / JZ-continue shape. That is why the function is small and heavily called: the compiler emitted the loop out of line once and inlined it where it was profitable.
sibling_analysis.analogue_evidence_label: the vtable scan and the symbol-table names are OBSERVED; the identification of the handle as a cursor is INFERRED from the two inlined duplicates and the two polarity witnesses

callees_evidence.form: CALL with ECX = self+0x8 and one stack word (the element); the callee ends in RET 0x4
callees_evidence.identified_operation: an acceptance test over an element. Its live 23-instruction body: ctx = element->f_8; if (ctx->vslot_0x2c() != 0) return 0; if ((uint)ctx->f_0xb58 >> 9 & 1) return 0; if ((byte)ctx->f_0x135 == 0) return 0; if (ctx->f_0x110 & 0x10) return 0; return 1. So it returns 1 only when all four conditions hold.
callees_evidence.identified: yes, mechanically. What any of the four conditions MEANS is not established, and the class behind ctx's slot +0x2c is not identified.

semantic_contract: Given a three-slot cursor handle {void** cursor; void** end; void* owner;}, this function advances the cursor to the first element the acceptance test accepts, and returns the handle. 1. It increments the handle's own cursor field by four bytes, i.e. by one pointer slot, so the element the handle started on is never re-examined (0x00b3d853). 2. It compares the advanced cursor against the end pointer for exact equality; on equality it stops immediately, without a final acceptance query (0x00b3d856-0x00b3d85b). 3. Otherwise it dereferences the cursor to obtain the element, loads the owner slot into ECX, and calls the acceptance port on the element (0x00b3d85d-0x00b3d863). 4. A zero answer sends it back to step 1; a non-zero answer ends the loop (0x00b3d868-0x00b3d86a). 5. Both exits return the receiver in EAX; the port's answer is never propagated (0x00b3d86c). Invariants: the only observable effect is the new value of the cursor field; the returned pointer always equals the receiver; the stack depth is constant across iterations because the port pops its own argument; the end test is equality and not ordering, so a handle whose cursor already equals its end will step past it and keep dereferencing, and the original relies on its callers to present a cursor strictly before the end; and the loop cannot terminate other than by exhausting the range or by finding an accepted element, so a port that always returns zero runs the handle off the end of its buffer.
classification_rationale: The complete 32-byte body, the ABI, the three field offsets, the do-while shape, the exact loop polarity and the single callee's full body were all read from the disassembly, and two callers were disassembled in full specifically to pin the polarity, each providing an independent witness. It is not STRONG_SEMANTIC because: (a) the ACCEPTANCE CRITERION is bounded - the port's four conditions are known mechanically but none of their meanings is established, and the class behind the context's vtable slot +0x2c was not identified, so what makes an element 'accepted' is unknown; (b) the receiver's own type is unresolved - the handle is a cursor over four-byte elements, but the element type and the owner's role are not established, and the owner slot is loaded into ECX and then never read by the port, so its purpose is genuinely open; (c) no SDK candidate exists for the class or the method, and the function is in no vtable (scan total=0), so nothing names it; and (d) 16 of the 18 canonical callers were not disassembled, so the range discipline its callers actually maintain is only sampled from two sites.
semantic_findings: The function is a compiler-emitted out-of-line copy of an advance-until-predicate loop. 0x00b41a40 and 0x00d66600 each contain an inlined fragment of the same loop, which is why it is only 32 bytes yet has 18 call sites.

The loop advances before it tests, so the handle's starting element is skipped by construction. This is the invariant a caller most easily gets wrong and it is invisible in the decompiled pseudocode, which reads as a do-while over *cursor.

The polarity is 'advance while the port returns zero', and that is the opposite of the naive reading of 'find the first matching element'. Two callers were disassembled specifically to settle it and both branch the same way: 0x00b41a60 TEST AL,AL / 0x00b41a62 JNZ skips the advance, and 0x00d66663 TEST AL,AL / 0x00d66665 JNZ does the same.

The end test is pointer equality, not ordering. Nothing in the body prevents the cursor from stepping past the end pointer, and the port would then be handed elements from beyond the range. The original depends entirely on its callers for that discipline.
The return is unconditionally the receiver. Every one of the 18 callers therefore either already holds the handle or ignores the result; the two inspected callers do the former.

The owner slot at +0x08 is loaded into ECX and never used, because the port reads its argument from the stack. Recording this as a dead load is the honest reading; inventing a reason for it would not be.
The port itself is a four-way conjunction of disqualifiers, so 'accepted' means the absence of four distinct conditions rather than the presence of one. It is a filter, not a matcher.
unresolved_questions: What is the element type? The handle's stride of four bytes and the unconditional dereference prove the elements are 4-byte values, but whether they are pointers, handles or indices is not established. The port treats its argument as a pointer to something with a field at +0x08, which is the only structural clue.

What is the owner at +0x08 for? It is loaded into ECX before the port call and the port never reads ECX. Either the port was inlined from something that did, or the owner is genuinely vestigial here. Not resolvable statically.

What do the port's four conditions mean? ctx->vslot_0x2c() must be zero, bit 9 of the dword at +0xb58 must be zero, the byte at +0x135 must be non-zero, and bit 4 of the byte at +0x110 must be zero. None of these is named in the SDK, and the four are read from an object this function never identifies.

What class does the ctx object belong to? The four field offsets (+0xb58, +0x135, +0x110) and a vtable slot at +0x2c describe a large Simulator object, but no vtable was located for it and the SDK offers no candidate, so the port's subject is unresolved.
Do all 18 callers maintain cursor < end on entry? Only the two inspected callers were checked, and both do. The other 16 were not, and the function has no guard.

Is the range [cursor, end) guaranteed to be non-empty? If a caller presents cursor == end the function walks off the buffer. Whether that ever happens in the shipping game is not determinable statically.

Why is the function at 0x00b3d850 rather than inlined everywhere? The 19 service accessors immediately below it suggest a different translation-unit or optimisation boundary, but the reason is not established.
runtime_gates: No original-process trace exists for 0x00b3d850; every claim is static.

A runtime trace would be needed to observe the element type, to see which of the port's four conditions actually rejects elements in play, and to check whether any caller ever presents a cursor equal to its end.
The identity of the ctx object and of its vtable slot +0x2c can only be resolved with a receiver whose vtable base is known at run time.
